headline: A calm week ended near the highs, Isaias came ashore weaker and east of the big refineries, and next week is the real test: bank and UnitedHealth earnings Tuesday, CPI Wednesday, TSMC Thursday, options expiration Friday.
summary: This is a weekend brief using Friday Oct 9 closing levels; markets are closed today. The S&P 500 rose 1.15% on the week to 7,811.54 and the Nasdaq 0.64% to 27,366.17, so Thursday's OpenAI revenue scare did not spread. Hurricane Isaias made landfall near Destin, Florida as a Category 2 late Friday, east of the Louisiana refining belt; damage reports for the two plants in its path (Chevron Pascagoula and Vertex Saraland) are the first thing to check Monday. Next week decides the regime: JPMorgan, Citi, Goldman, Wells Fargo, UnitedHealth and J&J report Tuesday Oct 13 before the open (Oct 13 is a Tuesday, not Monday), September CPI comes Wednesday with headline seen near 3.6%, TSMC reports Thursday, and monthly options expire Friday. Her MT Swing Setup scan came back to 44 names on Friday and now includes all seven dashboard swing setups, so the scanner and the dashboard agree again. The BDX put idea is removed: the live quote is thin and BDX dropped off her MT Put Candidates scan.

regime.why: Stocks are near highs and VIX is calm at 14.84, so breakouts tend to work. But the 10-year is still 5.24%, Brent is above $104, and the Fed has said another hike is possible; a hot core CPI on Wednesday would push that risk up. Keep normal size on confirmed breakouts, and avoid new entries in names that report next week.

signals.title: Isaias came ashore weaker and east of the big refineries; check two plants Monday
signals.what_happened: Isaias made landfall near Destin, Florida around 9:30pm ET Friday Oct 9 as a Category 2 with 105 mph winds, down from Category 3, then weakened over Alabama with nearly 900,000 customers without power. Before landfall, operators had shut in about 63% of US Gulf oil output (about 1.3 million barrels a day, BSEE via Quartz). The Louisiana refining belt was outside the path. The two plants in the path, Chevron Pascagoula and Vertex Saraland, together run about 466,000 barrels a day or 2.4% of US capacity; Chevron said Thursday Pascagoula was still running, and no damage report was out by Saturday morning. Brent settled at $104.72 on Friday.
signals.so_what: The storm premium in refiners and fuel prices should fade if Pascagoula reports no flooding and power returns quickly; analysts said a shut plant without damage needs one to two weeks to restart, so a power loss there is the main risk. Offshore wells usually restart within days once platforms are checked, which helps XOM and CVX volumes and clears the storm reason the last brief gave for waiting on their swing setups. Refiners (VLO, MPC) ran up on the threat and could give some back. Second order: lower diesel and jet risk helps airlines a little, but crude is still above $100 because of Hormuz, so Delta's $4.25 fuel assumption is not out of date. What would make this wrong: Monday reports of flooding or a long power outage at Pascagoula or Saraland, or a fresh Hormuz incident.

signals.title: Tuesday Oct 13: six big reports before the open, with UnitedHealth the one to watch for a clinician
signals.what_happened: JPMorgan, Citigroup, Goldman Sachs, Wells Fargo, UnitedHealth and Johnson & Johnson report before the open on Tuesday Oct 13; BlackRock, Bank of America and Morgan Stanley follow Wednesday Oct 14 per one roundup. Consensus: JPMorgan EPS about $5.90 on $51.5 billion revenue; Citigroup $2.66 on $23.7 billion; Goldman $15.39 on $17.42 billion, both down from a record Q2; UnitedHealth $4.12 on about $111.4 billion, with options pricing a move of about 8% either way. UnitedHealthcare's medical care ratio fell to 86.7% in Q2 from 89.4% a year earlier, helped by $860 million of favorable reserve development. On the dashboard (Oct 8 prices) JPM (331.42), C (128.08) and BLK (1,065.35) sit in Buy zone now, JNJ is Wait (price far above fair value), and GS fell 14.2% over the past month.
signals.so_what: Banks are the first real read on what 5.2% yields do: higher deposit costs against higher loan yields, and whether card and commercial credit losses are rising. Goldman's Q2 record and an Evercore read that third quarter deal and trading revenue tracked below estimates set a lower bar. UnitedHealth is the health care tone setter: its medical cost ratio tells you whether patients are using more care (hospital and outpatient volumes, Medicare Advantage utilization). A lower ratio supports CVS and CI, both Buy zone now on the dashboard; a jump would hit all managed care and help hospitals and device makers through higher volumes. Honest note: Buy zone verdicts on JPM, C and BLK use fundamentals and do not know about Tuesday; buying a day before earnings is a coin flip. What would make this wrong: a credit loss spike at JPM or a reserve release that flatters UNH's ratio.

signals.title: September CPI on Wednesday: gasoline lifts the headline, core decides the Oct 28 hike odds
signals.what_happened: September CPI is due Wednesday Oct 14 at 8:30am ET. Forecasts put the headline near 3.6% to 3.7% a year, up from 3.4%, with the Cleveland Fed nowcast (Oct 2) at 0.53% for the month and 3.60% for the year. Core is expected near 2.4% a year and about 0.2% for the month, down from 0.3% in August. The Fed raised rates on Sep 16 to 3.75% to 4.00% and meets again Oct 27 to 28. The 10-year closed the week at 5.24%, about 5 basis points lower.
signals.so_what: A gasoline driven headline is already expected, so the market will trade the core number. Core at 0.2% or below says the oil shock is not spreading into services, which would ease hike odds and help rate sensitive groups (homebuilders, small caps, long duration tech). Core at 0.3% or more with $104 Brent would raise Oct 28 hike odds and push the 10-year back toward its 5.35% high from Oct 5. For short puts: cash backing puts keeps earning a high T-bill rate either way. What would make this wrong: a surprise in shelter or medical services, which can swing core by itself.

signals.title: TSMC reports Thursday Oct 15 after a record quarter of sales; the call matters more than the numbers
signals.what_happened: TSMC already reported Q3 revenue of about NT$1.49 trillion, up about 51% from a year earlier and above the LSEG SmartEstimate of NT$1.46 trillion. September revenue was NT$511.86 billion, up 54.6% from a year ago and down 0.6% from August. Its Q3 guidance was US$44.6 to 45.8 billion with a 65% to 67% gross margin. The earnings call is Thursday Oct 15 at 2:00pm ET. TSM is Accumulate on pullback on the dashboard (457.99 on Oct 8, buy zone 377.58 to 443.65).
signals.so_what: Revenue is known, so the stock will move on Q4 guidance, 2027 capital spending and anything said about AI customer demand after OpenAI cut its own revenue figure to about $50 billion last week. A higher 2027 capex plan helps the tool and test suppliers on the AI compute theme (ASML, AMAT, KLAC, Advantest); a cautious tone would hit the debt funded builders (ORCL, CRWV) more than TSMC itself. Honest note: TSM is above its dashboard buy zone, so a good report is not a reason to chase. What would make this wrong: a margin miss from overseas fabs or a weaker dollar conversion.

signals.title: Innovation radar: enhanced geothermal moves up to early adoption as Fervo's first block sells power
signals.what_happened: Fervo Energy's first 33 MW GeoBlock at Cape Station, Utah synchronized with the grid on Sep 24, 2026 and declared commercial operation on Sep 30, one day before its contract date. It is the first utility scale enhanced geothermal plant selling power under contract. Two more blocks (about 100 MW in total for Phase I) are due by Jan 1, 2027, and a roughly 400 MW Phase II is under construction for 2028. The energy radar moves enhanced geothermal from pilot to early adoption on this evidence.
signals.so_what: Who pays: data center owners who want firm, carbon free power and will sign contracts near $100 to $130 per MWh. Who gets paid: the developer and the drillers, because enhanced geothermal is an oil field process (horizontal wells and fracking in hot rock). That makes rigs, frac crews and high temperature downhole tools the scarce input, which is a second market for HAL, SLB, NBR and HP as oil drilling slows. Honest note: one 33 MW block is a start, not scale; FRVO is a recent IPO with no dashboard verdict yet (not enough data), so this is a watch item. What would make this wrong: the next two blocks slip well past January, or wells lose heat faster than modeled.
